newsitem.title: MONACO: SOCCER-COACH TIGANA LOOKING FOR SUCCESS HE MISSED AS A PLAYER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COACH TIGANA LOOKING FOR SUCCESS HE MISSED AS A PLAYER.

text.p: For most French soccer fans the abiding memory of Jean Tigana is of the goal he created for Michel Platini in the last minute of extra time against Portugal in the semifinals of the 1984 European championship.
Tigana set up the winner by beating three players and squaring the ball across to skipper Platini.
Platini then appeared to take the ball in slow motion to score France's third goal in their famous 3-2 win on a sultry June night at Marseille's Velodrome Stadium.

It capped one of the great internationals of all time and France, boasting the brilliant midfield quartet of Platini, Tigana, Alain Giresse and Luis Fernandez, went on to beat Spain 2-0 in the final to become champions of Europe.

For Tigana, who was born in Mali and spent most of his playing days with Bordeaux, that was the peak of his dazzling career. He never tasted European success with his club, although his trophy cabinet was not entirely bare.
Under current French national team coach Aime Jacquet, Tigana won a French Cup and three league championship medals in the 1980s.
But now Tigana, the 41-year-old coach, is planning to achieve something Tigana the player never did -- win that elusive European club honour.
For he has moulded Monaco into a side brimming with such talent and style that they could well go on to win the UEFA Cup - something no French club has ever managed.

The way they demolished Newcastle United 4-0 on aggregate in their UEFA Cup quarter-final, together with earlier wins in the competition over Hamburg (aggregate 5-0) and Borussia Moenchengladbach (4-3), shows they can compete amongst the best -- and beat them.

"I hope we're going to get through to the final because as a player I often played in semifinals without reaching the final," Tigana said after Monaco's 3-0 second leg home victory over Newcastle on Tuesday.
Tigana played in European Cup and Cup Winners' Cup semifinals as well as two World Cup semifinals.
As a player alongside a dream-weaver like Platini, Tigana was a pragmatist -- winning the ball in midfield, battling for possession, laying off balls for others to convert into goals.
As a coach, he still retains a pragmatic approach, adding: "I'm not bothered about knowing who we're going to face in the semifinals or whether we'll be at home or away in the first leg.
"The important thing is what happens on the field. The rest is nothing more than literature, even if the players were magnificent," he said.
Tigana has galvanised the potential of a highly-skilled squad into a probable title-winning side after several near missess in the latter years of Arsene Wenger's period as coach with Monaco.
The club last won the French title in 1988 but are now seven points clear of the field and playing with a belief and confidence that almost gives them a goal start from the kick-off.
Tigana has built on the promise of the second half of last season, when Monaco made up lost ground to finish equal second on points behind Auxerre after a dismal start.
Now he works as hard on the mental aspects as the physical and technical qualities of his team with the full co-operation of a squad desperate for success.
His favourite phrase has become: "There is no reason to change course."
Even in defeat, Monaco are faithful to their style of play and it only requires a tweak in the mental attitude for the team to regain their winning form after a setback.

"The UEFA Cup is in large part a question of concentration, determination and mental attitude," said Tigana, who joined Monaco last season after coaching Lyon, one of his former clubs as a player, between 1993 and 1995.
Monaco dropped their guard in the second round after a brilliant 4-2 away leg victory against Borussia Moenchengladbach and lost the return 1-0, their only home defeat this season.

Tigana admitted the players had relaxed and he has since had to redress the balance in their concentration again after losing away in the league days before the away leg of their quarter-final first leg in Newcastle.

"We have the attacking potential and the organisation, but when you don't control the game, that's when you're in danger," said Tigana, who might have be given the national team job had it not gone to Jacquet in 1994. There are some now saying that when Jacquet eventually leaves the job, Tigana would be a likely successor.
Newcastle manager Kenny Dalglish was impressed by the qualities of the Monaco side, pointing to their organisation in defence and pace in attack.
Dalglish, who knows what it takes to win in Europe, said after Tuesday's match: "Monaco are the sort of team we can learn from. It has to be a very good side who can beat them."
